clinicalPearls: Characterised by abnormally lax, rubbery upper eyelids that evert with minimal traction, exposing a papillary conjunctivitis on the upper tarsus
Symptoms of irritation, redness, and discharge are typically worse on waking and often worse on the side the patient sleeps on
Strongly associated with obesity and obstructive sleep apnoea, which should be actively sought
Thought to result from loss of tarsal elastin, allowing spontaneous nocturnal eversion of the lid against the pillow
Often under-recognised because the everted lid returns to its normal position by the time of examination unless laxity is specifically tested
Conservative management includes nocturnal eye shielding or taping and ocular lubrication to protect the exposed surface
Treating coexisting obstructive sleep apnoea, for example with continuous positive airway pressure, is an important part of management
Surgical horizontal lid tightening is considered for symptoms refractory to conservative measures
reference.pathophysiology: The disorder involves a marked reduction in elastin and altered connective tissue within the tarsal plate, rendering the upper eyelid abnormally lax. During sleep the floppy lid everts spontaneously where it contacts the pillow, so the palpebral conjunctiva is exposed and mechanically rubbed through the night, producing a chronic papillary conjunctivitis and surface drying. Recurrent mechanical stress together with systemic factors such as obesity and obstructive sleep apnoea, with intermittent hypoxia and increased tissue matrix-metalloproteinase activity, is thought to drive the elastin degradation.
additionalDifferentials: Giant papillary conjunctivitis, for example contact lens related
Involutional lid laxity with ectropion or entropion
additionalInvestigations: Clinical demonstration of eyelid laxity with easy eversion and distraction testing
Slit-lamp examination for papillary conjunctivitis, punctate keratopathy, and corneal changes including keratoconus
Fluorescein staining to assess ocular surface integrity
Screening questionnaire and referral for a sleep study to detect obstructive sleep apnoea
Assessment of body mass index and cardiovascular risk
Corneal topography where keratoconus is suspected
redFlags: Corneal ulceration, infiltrate, or thinning threatening vision
Undiagnosed obstructive sleep apnoea with daytime somnolence and cardiovascular risk
Persistent unilateral disease raising suspicion of an alternative cause
reference.prognosis: Symptoms usually improve substantially with nocturnal lid protection and treatment of sleep apnoea; surgical lid tightening is effective for refractory cases, but the condition may recur and the associated systemic disease carries its own morbidity.
pitfalls: Failing to test eyelid laxity, so the diagnosis is missed and the eye is treated as ordinary conjunctivitis
Not screening for obstructive sleep apnoea, leaving significant systemic disease undiagnosed
Relying on topical treatment alone without protecting the lid at night
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology Basic and Clinical Science Course (Oculoplastics)
management: Nocturnal eyelid protection with shielding or taping to prevent spontaneous lid eversion against the pillow
Ocular surface lubrication with artificial tears and ointment to protect the exposed conjunctiva and cornea
Identification and treatment of obstructive sleep apnoea with continuous positive airway pressure, alongside weight reduction
Surgical horizontal eyelid tightening for refractory or severe laxity
Monitoring for and management of associated corneal disease including keratoconus and punctate keratopathy
Referral for a sleep study and ophthalmology or oculoplastics follow-up
